transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-01
Start: 14:30 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Anika (Redwood SE), Priya (Lodestar), Tomás (Lodestar SRE), Ellen (Lodestar Security)

Summary: initial discovery to understand Lodestar's VPC onramp needs, scaling expectations, and data residency/sovereignty constraints for Redwood Private. Discussed private endpoints, VPC peering options, transit gateway patterns, egress IP requirements, and a rough pilot plan.

[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone uh thanks for joining, um I'm Jordan from Redwood. With me today is Anika (she's our solutions engineer) - we're excited to get a sense of Lodestar's constraints and timeline.
[00:22] Priya Venkataraman: Hi Jordan, thanks. We want to understand the onramp for private deployment, especially scaling, where data needs to live, and how egress is controlled. We have some regulatory boundaries for EU and APAC.
[00:40] Anika Rao: Great, that helps. Quick housekeeping: we'll cover network topology options (peering, private endpoints, transit options), model routing & capacity (dedicated vs hosted vs private), and then capture action items. If anything's too deep we'll book a follow-up deep dive.
[01:05] Tomás Ruiz: Quick note - we're particularly sensitive to IP allowlists, we run strict firewall rules and NAT IPs, so stable egress is a must. Also low variability on latency, our product needs sub-100ms p50 for inference calls.
[01:30] Ellen Cho: And on my side, encryption at rest, KMS integration, and audit logs - we'll need SOC2 evidence and an architecture diagram that shows no data plane egress to public internet for EU data.
[01:50] Jordan Patel: Understood. At a high level, Redwood Private can be deployed in your VPC with private endpoints so the data plane stays in your network. We support VPC peering and transit gateway attachments depending on cloud. For egress we can use a pool of fixed NAT IPs in a customer-managed NAT or provide static egress via our private egress nodes — though that depends on contract for Dedicated/Private.
[02:20] Priya Venkataraman: Can you explain the difference between the peering and private endpoint approaches? We have a pretty locked down VPC so opening peering requires security review.
[02:45] Anika Rao: Sure. VPC peering is direct routing between AWS VPCs (or the equivalent) so traffic flows over the cloud backbone. Private endpoints (privatelink/privatelink-like) use an endpoint service - usually easier to restrict to specific services but adds a managed endpoint in the customer VPC. Peering is simpler network-wise but can complicate IP overlap and routing policies. Private endpoints are often preferred for strict security models because they present an interface in your VPC.
[03:15] Tomás Ruiz: IP overlap is a real concern - we have overlapping subnets across regions and accounts. How do you handle that?
[03:30] Anika Rao: We typically ask for a non-overlapping /16 or /20 allocation for the Redwood side inside the peering or we recommend using PrivateLink where you don't need to route our IPs directly—so no peering-level overlap. Another pattern is transit with NAT translation, but that adds indirection and can affect latency.
[04:05] Priya Venkataraman: Ok. Around regions: we keep EU production data in eu-west-1 and have a separate APAC tenancy in ap-southeast-1. Can Redwood run private nodes in our chosen regions?
[04:25] Jordan Patel: Yes - Redwood Private supports region-specific deployments. For EU-only data we can deploy control plane in a Redwood-managed control plane in-us or you can opt for our customer-managed control plane. For on-prem or fully air-gapped we have an on-prem package but that is a separate process. The key is we need to align on KMS, routing, and any regulatory audit controls.
[04:55] Ellen Cho: When you say control plane, does that mean metadata leaves our environment? We can't have tokens or user prompts sent outside EU boundaries for certain workloads.
[05:12] Anika Rao: Good point. There's two models: 1) Redwood-managed control plane that can be region-restricted (we can offer EU-only control plane for Enterprise deals), or 2) a private control plane deployed into your VPC/tenant so metadata and control signals never leave your environment. We'll need to confirm which workloads fall into the EU-scope.
[05:40] Tomás Ruiz: Performance-wise, how does the private deployment compare to dedicated hosted? We're trying to balance cost and SLOs.
[05:55] Jordan Patel: In many cases performance is similar to dedicated; the main difference is networking - if you introduce additional NAT/transit hops that can add 10-30ms variability. Also hardware choices (GPU type, quantization) impact avg latency. Our SE team can propose a baseline instance configuration.
[06:20] Priya Venkataraman: Is it possible to use Redwood Dedicated inside our VPC so we get reserved capacity plus the private network?
[06:35] Anika Rao: Yes you can do Dedicated capacity attached to your VPC. That's a common pattern: reserved GPU pools that are network-isolated. It tends to be the sweet spot for customers that need predictable throughput and private data control.
[06:55] Ellen Cho: For compliance, we need to see audit logs for every inference request and key rotation events. Does Redwood provide request-level logging and KMS integration?
[07:12] Jordan Patel: We do provide detailed request tracing and audit logs via the console and can forward logs to your SIEM via syslog or S3. KMS integration is supported for data-at-rest keys; for private deployments we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS or HSM) depending on the package.
[07:40] Tomás Ruiz: Are there known limitations on throughput when you run in a private mode? We might spike to 2000 concurrent inference qps in peak.
[07:55] Anika Rao: Capacity is mostly constrained by GPU compute and batching efficiency. In a private/dedicated deployment, you can provision more instances and autoscale. We'll help size the pool; typical approach is run a small pilot with representative traffic to tune batching and GPU types. For 2k QPS we'd probably recommend multiple GPU nodes with optimized kernels and continuous batching.
[08:30] Priya Venkataraman: What about prefix/KV cache concerns - we can't leak cached prefixes between tenants.
[08:42] Anika Rao: All customer workloads are isolated; KV caches are scoped per-tenant. In private mode we'd ensure strict namespace separation. There may be ephemeral caches on the same host but they're logically isolated; we can describe the isolation model in the security pack.
[09:05] Priya Venkataraman: Great. Can you outline the pilot? Timeline?
[09:18] Jordan Patel: Typical pilot flow: 1) discovery + network intake (this call) 2) security review + exchange of network details 3) short pilot — often 2 weeks — with representative load and a small dataset 4) evaluation and then a production roll if good. For network, we'll need: allowed egress IPs, VPC CIDRs, any proxy rules, and the person who will test connectivity.
[09:50] Tomás Ruiz: We'll need to run synthetic latency tests. Do you have a recommended test harness?
[09:58] Anika Rao: Yes we'll share a lightweight harness and some terraform snippets to spin up endpoints and run steady qps. It obs — the transcription tech sometimes garbles — it includes a sample gRPC load generator and a tokenized prompt set for functional checks.
[10:25] Ellen Cho: Regarding egress, does Redwood require any public internet egress from our environment during normal operation? We want zero public egress for EU workloads.
[10:40] Jordan Patel: For Private with customer-managed control plane and private endpoints, no. We can keep the data plane fully internal. The only exception is if you want to use Redwood-hosted model catalog updates or telemetry — that can be optional and configured to route via a proxy or go through your approved egress path.
[11:05] Priya Venkataraman: Ok that helps. A bit more detail on the peering/NAT IP situation: we currently map outbound traffic through a small set of NAT gateways with fixed Elastic IPs per region. Will that work?
[11:20] Anika Rao: Yes, fixed EIPs are ideal. If you want Redwood to accept traffic to private endpoints, we prefer a stable set of IPs on our side too, so both sides can be allowlisted. We'll provide our side's IPs for the peer session or endpoint connections.
[11:45] Tomás Ruiz: Any gotchas with cross-account peering? We often have multiple AWS accounts and SCPs (service control policies) that block certain peering causes.
[12:00] Anika Rao: Cross-account peering can be more complex — you'll need the accounts to accept peering and certain routes to be propagated. PrivateLink avoids some of that because it relies on endpoint services rather than peering rules. We'll document the IAM and SCP changes you might need.
[12:30] Priya Venkataraman: Are there additional costs for PrivateLink endpoints?
[12:38] Jordan Patel: There's typical cloud charges for endpoints — yes. And there may be additional Redwood licensing for fully private on-prem packages. We'll call those out in the pricing doc.
[12:55] Priya Venkataraman: For control plane residency, can we host the control plane in our VPC? Who manages upgrades then?
[13:10] Anika Rao: You can choose customer-managed control plane. Redwood provides an ops package that includes upgrade runbooks and a managed services option. If you self-manage we'll hand over the upgrade tooling and docs; Redwood can also run upgrades on a schedule if you want the managed route.
[13:35] Tomás Ruiz: How disruptive are upgrades to running inference? We need near-zero disruption.
[13:42] Anika Rao: We design rolling upgrades with canaries and automatic fallback. For critical workloads we'll coordinate maintenance windows. Most upgrades are non-disruptive given proper load balancing across nodes.
[14:05] Jordan Patel: Quick question from our side — what is your expected timeline for a pilot and full rollout?
[14:12] Priya Venkataraman: We're targeting a pilot by mid-December and production in Q1 2028 but that's flexible if security approvals take longer. The budget window opens early January.
[14:30] Jordan Patel: Good — that aligns with our typical lead time. We'll try to get the network checklist to you quickly so you can start approvals.
[14:45] Tomás Ruiz: One last technical point: we do some on-prem inference for latency-sensitive customers; would Redwood's on-prem package require hardware procurement on our side or can you supply the appliance?
[14:57] Anika Rao: We have both models. For on-prem / air-gapped, we have a partner program and an appliance offering. Hardware procurement is often done by the customer but we can provide an approved spec and partner assistance. That would be a separate proposal.
[15:20] Ellen Cho: Security evidence - can you share SOC2 Type II and penetration test reports and details on how audit logs are stored and retained?
[15:33] Jordan Patel: Yes we'll attach the security pack after the call - it includes SOC2 artifacts, pen test summaries, and an explanation of our audit log retention. For private deployments the log forwarding options will be documented.
[15:50] Priya Venkataraman: Cool. Are there any known region constraints, like models not available in certain regions?
[16:02] Anika Rao: Some open model runtimes may be limited by container images or specific kernel availability on certain GPU instance types. We validate model availability per-region during onboarding and can propose quantized variants if a GPU type is constrained.
[16:30] Tomás Ruiz: Can you talk about fallback behavior if a region is overloaded? Do you failover to another region? That might violate data residency.
[16:45] Jordan Patel: We have routing policies per workload; you can pin a workload to a region and opt out of cross-region failover. For failovers that cross region, we'd discuss data residency implications first. Automatic failover is typically disabled for residency-bound workloads.
[17:10] Priya Venkataraman: Perfect. Let's talk briefly about the test we'll run — we'd like to run both p50/p95 latency tests and some quality checks, about 10k prompts.
[17:25] Anika Rao: That sounds good. We'll send the harness and a suggested prompt set. Also a note — sometimes transcripts and docs use different nomenclature, so we'll include a glossary for terms like KV cache, prefix caching, private link, etc.
[17:50] Tomás Ruiz: Lastly - for IAM and service accounts, do you need a particular role or cert to be present in our account for onramp?
[18:02] Anika Rao: Usually we ask for a cross-account IAM role with limited permissions if we need to create endpoints or route tables on your behalf. Alternatively you can run our terraform snippets and grant us read-only auditing access. We'll provide both options.
[18:30] Jordan Patel: Alright wrapping up - recap and next steps: 1) Jordan sends VPC peering checklist and architecture note, 2) Lodestar shares region/residency spreadsheet + egress IPs, 3) Anika schedules technical deep dive and shares benchmark harness. Any additions?
[18:55] Priya Venkataraman: That's it from us. Thanks, Jordan and Anika.
[19:05] Ellen Cho: Thanks. We'll look for the security pack and the network checklist.
[19:12] Jordan Patel: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up by email with the attachments and proposed times for the deep dive.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings present (e.g., privet private, K-V cash, transit way) — please refer to technical doc attachments for definitive terms. Links shared during call: Security pack (link sent after call), Network intake template (to be shared).
